99.title: The pause
99.hook: the moment at the top and bottom
99.howItsDone: In Hindu yoga traditions, kumbhaka, breath retention, is taught gradually by a teacher; beginners learn short, soft pauses after the in-breath and out-breath before any longer holds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, slow it down: four counts in, six counts out. Your line was longer out. Did you try three rounds before answering someone? Today, the place between the breaths. Day ninety-nine.

Throw a ball straight up. Watch it. It rises, slows, and then, for a split second at the very top, it stops. Not rising, not falling. Just hanging there. Then it comes down. Your breath does the same thing, thousands of times a day. At the top of the in-breath, there's a tiny moment before the out-breath starts. At the bottom of the out-breath, another one, before the next breath comes. Most of us have never noticed them. Today, you're going to find them.
screen: `A BALL AT THE TOP OF ITS ARC.` → `THE BREATH HAS A TOP, TOO.` → `AND A BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The word is kumbhaka. It comes from kumbha, a pot, a clay water jar. The picture is the breath held still, like water resting in a pot. The old yoga texts, like the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, written down more than five hundred years ago, treat kumbhaka as the heart of breath practice, and describe long, powerful holds. We're not doing that. Those were taught one to one, by a teacher who watched the student closely. Today is the gentlest version there is. There are two pauses. One at the top, after the in-breath, called antara, inner. One at the bottom, after the out-breath, called bahya, outer. The Yoga Sutras name both, calling the inner one abhyantara. And there's a third kind the tradition talks about, a pause that happens on its own, without effort, when the mind goes very still. The texts call it kevala, alone, and describe it as where the practice is heading. So, how to do it safely. Breathe in, and at the top, rest for a count of two. No clamping the throat, no straining. Just a soft stop, like the ball at the top of its arc. Breathe out, long. At the bottom, rest for two. Then let the next breath come when it wants. If a pause ever makes you feel anxious or short of air, skip it and breathe normally. If you're pregnant, or have high blood pressure, or a heart or lung condition, leave the holds out entirely and just notice where the pauses would be. Noticing is enough. The still point is already there.
screen: `KUMBHA — A WATER JAR.` · `A PAUSE AT THE TOP, AND THE BOTTOM.` · `THE ONE THAT HAPPENS ON ITS OWN.` · `TWO COUNTS, NEVER A STRAIN.` · then, large: `THE STILL POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gentle holds. Sit tall and soft. Take a few ordinary breaths. Now breathe in, four counts, and at the top, rest: one, two. Breathe out, six counts, and at the bottom, rest: one, two. Then let the next breath come. If the holds feel easy, keep them. If not, just notice where the top and bottom are, without stopping. Either way is the practice. Look for the still point, like the ball hanging in the air. The bell holds the time.
Kumbhaka. From kumbha, a water jar. The pause in the breath, held gently at the top or the bottom.
Your line: the still point. Today, find it outside the breath too: the second between putting down one thing and picking up the next. Rest there, once. Day ninety-nine.

100.title: One nostril
100.howItsDone: In Hindu yoga practice, nadi shodhana, alternate-nostril breathing using the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, is a common daily pranayama, often done before meditation or mantra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kumbhaka: the soft pause at the top and bottom of the breath. Your line was the still point. Did you find it between two things? Today is day one hundred. And we use one nostril at a time. Day one hundred.

Try this right now. Put a finger under your nose and breathe out gently. Then check each side. Chances are, one nostril is a little more open than the other. That's not a cold. It's normal. Throughout the day, your body quietly shifts which side does more of the work, back and forth, every few hours. Doctors call it the nasal cycle. You've been doing it your whole life without knowing. Yoga has a practice that works with exactly those two sides.
screen: `ONE SIDE IS MORE OPEN.` → `IT SWITCHES EVERY FEW HOURS.` → `YOGA WORKS WITH BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: The practice is called nadi shodhana. Nadi means a channel, a stream. In yoga's picture of the body, prana, the life-force, moves through channels, the way water moves through streams. Shodhana means cleansing, clearing. So: clearing the channels. The texts describe three main channels. Ida, on the left, linked to the moon, cooling. Pingala, on the right, linked to the sun, warming. And sushumna, in the center, along the spine. Breathing through one side and then the other, the old teachers said, brings the two into balance. You don't have to take that map literally to try the practice. Here's how, safely. Raise your right hand. Fold your index and middle fingers down toward the palm. Now your thumb can close the right nostril, and your ring finger can close the left. Close the right side with your thumb, and breathe in through the left. Close the left with your ring finger, open the right, breathe out through the right. Breathe in through the right. Close it, open the left, breathe out through the left. That's one round. In left, out right, in right, out left. Gentle, slow, no holding. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika teaches this with long holds. We leave those out. If your nose is blocked, skip it today, and just picture the breath moving side to side. If you get lightheaded, stop. One nostril at a time, and the whole thing finds its balance.
screen: `NADI, A CHANNEL. SHODHANA, CLEARING.` · `IDA, LEFT. PINGALA, RIGHT.` · `THUMB AND RING FINGER.` · `IN LEFT, OUT RIGHT, IN RIGHT, OUT LEFT.` · then, large: `BALANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: alternate-nostril breathing. Right hand up, index and middle fingers folded. Thumb closes the right side. Breathe in through the left, slowly. Ring finger closes the left, thumb lifts. Breathe out through the right. In through the right. Switch. Out through the left. That's one round. Keep going at your own pace, soft and even. If you lose track of which side, it's fine: just breathe out, and start again on the left. The bell holds the time.
Nadi shodhana. Clearing the channels. Breathing one nostril at a time, left and right, into balance.
Your line: balance. Once today, before a meeting or before sleep, do five slow rounds, left and right, and notice if anything evens out. Day one hundred.

101.title: The bee
101.howItsDone: In Hindu yoga practice, bhramari, the humming bee breath, is done by breathing in through the nose and humming on the out-breath, often with the ears closed by the thumbs; it's commonly used before meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadi shodhana: one nostril at a time, left and right. Your line was balance. Did anything even out? Today, the breath makes a sound. Day one hundred one.

Two in the morning, a parent rocking a baby that won't settle, and a sound comes out. Not a song, exactly. Just a low hum, mmm, over and over. Or the hum you make without noticing when you're concentrating, or stirring a pot. People hum to settle things. The yoga tradition took that hum and turned it into a breath practice. It named it after an insect that buzzes around flowers.
screen: `A PARENT HUMMING AT 2AM.` → `WE HUM TO SETTLE THINGS.` → `YOGA NAMED IT AFTER A BEE.`

segments.voice: The word is bhramari. It comes from bhramara, a bee, the big dark kind that drones around flowers. Bhramari is the bee breath. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes it with two bee sounds: a quick in-breath that buzzes like a male bee, and a slow out-breath that hums like a female bee. Many teachers today keep only the second half: a quiet in-breath, and a long hum out. That's the version here, and it's simple enough that you can feel it working in your own head. Here's how. Sit tall. Close your lips gently, teeth slightly apart, jaw loose. Breathe in through the nose. Then, as you breathe out, hum. A steady, low mmm, for as long as the out-breath lasts, without forcing it. Feel where the sound goes. Maybe the lips tingle. Maybe the face buzzes, or the whole skull seems to hum from the inside. Then breathe in again, quietly, and hum again. If you want to go further, there's a traditional way to turn the sound inward. Put your thumbs gently on the little flaps at the front of your ears, and close them. Now the hum is almost all inside, and the room disappears. Some teachers add the fingers over the eyes, too. Keep the pressure light. Notice the connection to the last few days. The hum makes the out-breath longer, naturally, without counting. Longer out. And when the hum ends, there's a still point before the next breath. The week is building on itself. And the easiest instruction in all of yoga: hum.
screen: `BHRAMARA, A BEE.` · `BREATHE IN, HUM OUT.` · `THUMBS ON THE EAR FLAPS.` · `THE HUM MAKES THE OUT-BREATH LONG.` · then, large: `HUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the bee breath. Sit tall, lips gently closed, jaw loose. Breathe in through the nose. Now hum on the out-breath, low and steady, mmm, until it runs out. Breathe in quietly. Hum again. If you'd like, press the ear flaps closed with your thumbs and hear the hum inside. If you're somewhere you can't make noise, hum silently, and feel the lips tingle anyway. Keep it easy. After a few rounds, let the humming stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves. The bell holds the time.
Bhramari. From bhramara, the bee. Breathing in, and humming out like one.
Your line: hum. Today, when you catch yourself tense, hum one long out-breath. In the car, in the shower, under your breath at your desk. Day one hundred one.

102.title: The victorious breath
102.hook: the ocean sound from yoga class explained
102.howItsDone: In Hindu yoga traditions, ujjayi is breathing through the nose with a slight narrowing of the throat that makes a soft ocean sound; it's used in seated pranayama and throughout many styles of posture practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhramari, the bee: breathe in, hum out. Your line was hum. Where did you catch yourself humming? Today, another sound, and this one you may have heard in a yoga class. Day one hundred two.

If you've ever been to a yoga class, you may have heard it. The room goes quiet, everyone's moving slowly, and there's a sound filling the space, soft and rushing, like waves on a beach far away. It's coming from everyone at once. Like a whole room gently snoring, wide awake. The teacher probably called it ocean breath, and maybe never explained what's actually going on. Today, the explanation. And a surprisingly big name for a small sound.
screen: `A QUIET ROOM, A ROOM OF WAVES.` → `OCEAN BREATH.` → `A BIG NAME FOR A SMALL SOUND.`

segments.voice: Ujjayi is usually translated as victorious. It comes from ud, upward, and ji, to conquer, to win. The same root as the name Vijay, victory. Why victorious? Teachers explain it different ways. Some say it's the breath that rises up and wins mastery over the rest. Some say it simply means the breath of one who has won. The texts don't settle it, so we won't pretend to. What's clear is how it's done. At the back of your throat is the glottis, the opening your voice comes through. In ujjayi, you narrow it very slightly, as if you were about to whisper. The air rubbing past it makes that soft, ocean sound. Here's the easiest way to find it. Open your mouth, and breathe out as if you were fogging up a mirror. Haaa. Feel that slight catch in the throat? Now close your mouth, and keep that same catch as you breathe out through the nose. There it is. The ocean. Then try it on the in-breath, too. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes ujjayi with the mouth closed, drawing the breath in through both nostrils so that it sounds in the throat. Why do it? The sound gives your attention something to hold. It slows the breath on its own. And you can use it anywhere: sitting, walking, in a yoga pose. Two cautions. It should be soft. If people across the room can hear you, it's too much. And the throat stays relaxed, never squeezed. The ocean in your throat.
screen: `UD, UPWARD. JI, TO WIN.` · `A SLIGHT NARROWING IN THE THROAT.` · `FOG THE MIRROR, THEN CLOSE YOUR MOUTH.` · `SOFT, NEVER SQUEEZED.` · then, large: `THE OCEAN IN YOUR THROAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the victorious breath. Sit tall. Open your mouth and breathe out as if fogging a mirror, haaa. Do it once more. Now close your mouth and keep the same soft catch in the throat as you breathe out through your nose. Hear the ocean. Breathe in the same way, a quiet rushing. Let it be slow, and let the out-breath be a little longer. Keep the sound gentle, only loud enough for you. Just listen to the waves. The bell holds the time.
Ujjayi. The victorious breath. A soft ocean sound, made by narrowing the throat just slightly.
Your line: the ocean in your throat. Today, on a walk or in a waiting room, take five ujjayi breaths, so quiet nobody else could hear them. Day one hundred two.

103.title: Your breath routine
103.howItsDone: Many Hindus who practice yoga do a short daily pranayama sequence, often in the early morning before meditation or puja, combining slow breathing, alternate-nostril breathing and humming or ujjayi breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ujjayi: the victorious breath, the ocean in your throat. Did you take five quiet ones? Today, the end of breath week, and you put all six pieces together. Day one hundred three.

Six days ago you knew how to breathe the way everybody does: without thinking. Since then you've watched the breath. Slowed it down. Found the pause at the top and bottom. Breathed one nostril at a time. Hummed like a bee. Made the ocean in your throat. That's a real toolkit, explained piece by piece. Today we don't add anything new. We put it together into one short routine you can do every morning, in about five minutes.
screen: `SIX DAYS, SIX PIECES.` → `NOTHING NEW TODAY.` → `ONE ROUTINE, FIVE MINUTES.`

segments.voice: The word for all of it is pranayama. Prana, the breath and life-force you met on the first day. And ayama, which means extending, stretching out. So pranayama is lengthening the breath. Some read it instead as prana plus yama, restraint, reining the breath in. Scholars and teachers read it both ways, and both describe what you've been doing. In the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, pranayama is the fourth of the eight limbs of yoga. It comes after posture and before turning the senses inward. So in the classic picture, it's a doorway: from the body into stillness. Here's your five minutes, in order. One. Watch the breath, thirty seconds, no changes. That's prana. Two. Four in, six out, for a minute. Slow it down. Three. Add the soft pause, two counts at the top and bottom, for a few rounds, only if it's comfortable. Kumbhaka. Four. Alternate nostrils, five rounds. Nadi shodhana. Five. Three long hums. Bhramari. Six. Finish with a minute of ujjayi, and let it fade into ordinary breathing, and just sit. That's it. The order goes from noticing, to shaping, to sound, to stillness. You don't have to do all six every day. On a rushed morning, two of them is a routine. What matters is that it's yours, and that you come back to it. This is the first piece of the daily practice you're building across this camp. Five minutes, yours.
screen: `PRANA, AND AYAMA — LENGTHENING.` · `THE FOURTH LIMB OF YOGA.` · `WATCH, SLOW, PAUSE, SIDES, HUM, OCEAN.` · `NOTICING, SHAPING, SOUND, STILLNESS.` · then, large: `FIVE MINUTES, YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the short version of your routine, to fit the bell. Sit tall and soft. Watch three breaths, just as they are. Now four in, six out, three times. Now three rounds of alternate nostrils: in left, out right, in right, out left. Now one long hum, mmm. Now close your mouth and find the ocean, soft, for a few breaths. Then let all of it go, and just sit, breathing however it wants to. Tomorrow morning, try the full five minutes on your own. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama. Prana, breath and life; ayama, lengthening. The practice of the breath, and the fourth limb of yoga.
Your line: five minutes, yours. Pick a time for it tomorrow, after brushing your teeth, before coffee, and set it there, like an appointment. Day one hundred three.

104.title: Choosing yours
104.howItsDone: Many Hindus have a personal mantra tied to their ishta devata, their chosen form of God; in many lineages it is given privately by a guru at initiation (diksha), while others inherit a family deity's mantra or are drawn to one over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama: your breath routine, six pieces in five minutes. Your line was five minutes, yours. Did you set a time for it? This week, we add words to the breath: mantra. Day one hundred four.

Ask a few Hindu grandmothers what they say under their breath while they cook, or wait for the bus, or can't sleep. One will say Ram, Ram, Ram. Another, Om Namah Shivaya. Another will smile and not tell you, because hers was given to her quietly years ago, and it's private. Almost everyone has one. Not the only one they know. The one that's theirs. The one they go back to at 3am without thinking. Where does that come from? And how does anyone find theirs?
screen: `RAM, RAM, RAM.` → `ONE SHE WON'T TELL YOU.` → `THE ONE THAT'S THEIRS.`

segments.voice: The word is ishta. It means desired, cherished, the one you love and choose. You'll hear it most in the phrase ishta devata, your chosen form of God. Remember from the first weeks: Hindus often speak of one divine reality with many faces. Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna, Rama, the Goddess, Ganesha. The idea of the ishta devata is that a person is drawn to one face in particular, and it's as if that face were drawn to them. Many Hindus say that face finds you as much as you find it. So a person's mantra usually belongs to their ishta. A devotee of Shiva says Shiva's name. A devotee of Krishna, Krishna's. How is it chosen? In many lineages, you don't choose it at all. A guru gives it to you, in a ceremony called diksha, initiation, and it's kept private. Some families have a family deity, and the mantra comes with the family. And some people simply try, and notice which one their heart keeps returning to. All three are real paths, and different teachers hold them differently. This week, you'll meet four mantras that are sung openly, in temples and homes, by millions: for Shiva, for Ganesha, for Krishna, and the Gayatri. Try them all. You're not being asked to pick a god. You're noticing which sound settles you. Some Hindus would say that noticing is the ishta beginning to show itself. One that fits.
screen: `ISHTA — CHOSEN, CHERISHED.` · `ONE FACE THAT DRAWS YOU.` · `GIVEN, INHERITED, OR FOUND.` · `FOUR MANTRAS THIS WEEK.` · then, large: `ONE THAT FITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try three. Sit, and take a few slow breaths from your routine. Now say, softly or silently, Om. Just the sound, three times, on the out-breath. Notice how it sits. Now Ram, the name of Rama, three times. Notice. Now Shanti, peace, three times. Notice. You don't have to believe anything to try them. Just listen for which one your body wants to say a fourth time. Then say that one, slowly, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Ishta. Chosen, cherished. The face of God a person is drawn to, and the mantra that comes with it.
Your line: one that fits. Today, the next time you're waiting, say the one you picked, silently, three times. See if it comes back on its own later. Day one hundred four.

105.title: Om namah shivaya
105.hook: the five syllables; what they point at
105.howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva chant Om Namah Shivaya daily, often 108 times on a mala of rudraksha beads, and sing it through the night on Maha Shivaratri; it is widely chanted openly, though some lineages also give it formally at initiation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ishta: the chosen one, and the mantra that comes with it. Your line was one that fits. Did the one you picked come back on its own? Today, the first of four mantras: Shiva's. Day one hundred five.

You heard it on Shivaratri, the great night: temples full until dawn, and one sound rolling through them, over and over. Om Namah Shivaya. In the world of Shiva, it's everywhere. You'll find it painted on trucks in India, carved over temple doors, whispered by people who've said it all their lives, and sung by people who just learned it. It's short. It's easy to say. And it has a hidden count inside it. Five syllables, and each one, people say, is doing something.
screen: `THE SOUND OF SHIVARATRI.` → `ON TRUCKS, ON TEMPLE DOORS.` → `FIVE SYLLABLES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Take off the Om at the front, and count what's left. Na. Mah. Shi. Vaa. Ya. Five syllables. That's why it's called the panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra. Om is the sound we met on the very first days, the whole of reality in one breath. Namah means I bow. Shivaya means to Shiva. So: Om, I bow to Shiva. It's very old. In the Yajur Veda, in a long hymn called the Shri Rudram, you'll find the words namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: bow to the auspicious one, and to the more auspicious. Tradition hears the mantra's root there. And the name Shiva itself means kind, auspicious, the one who brings good. Now, what does it point at? Here's where teachers have gone deep. In the Shaiva tradition of the south, the five syllables are often matched to the five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space. So saying it is like naming the whole world and bowing to what's in all of it. Others hear the five as five things Shiva does: creating, sustaining, dissolving, hiding and revealing. And there's an old wordplay people love: namah heard as na mama, not mine. Bowing means: this isn't about me. Different teachers hold different meanings, and nobody has to pick one. One picture many share is where it leads: Shiva as the great yogi, sitting utterly still on the mountain. Saying his name is bowing to that stillness. Your line puts it simply. I bow to the stillness.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: japa, twenty-seven times. Japa means repeating a mantra, counting as you go. Twenty-seven is a quarter of a full mala, a string of prayer beads. If you have beads, use them. If not, use your fingers: touch each finger joint with your thumb as you go. Sit, breathe once or twice from your routine. Then, softly, on the out-breath: Om Namah Shivaya. One. Again: two. Let it be slow. If you don't pray, just let it be sound, and count. When you reach twenty-seven, stop, and sit in what's left. The bell holds the time.
Om namah shivaya. Om, I bow to Shiva. Five syllables, na mah shi vaa ya, bowing to the stillness.
Your line: I bow to the stillness. Today, when you catch a still moment, the kettle before it boils, the car before you get out, bow to it, just inside. Day one hundred five.
